title: Micro Effects of Macro Announcements: Real-Time Price Discovery in Foreign Exchange
author: Andersen, Bollerslev, Diebold, Vega
source_type: journal (American Economic Review 93(1), 2003; NBER WP 8959, May 2002)
summary: High-frequency USD spot rates against DEM, GBP, JPY, CHF and EUR over six years with survey expectations: announcement surprises produce conditional-mean jumps; the response depends on timing and the sign of the surprise; bad news has greater impact than good news.
extracted_hypotheses: Announcement windows (e.g. 08:30 ET US releases) are distinct regimes for USD/JPY and GBP/USD; surprise sign matters
methodology: Real-time quotes, announcement surprises vs survey expectations
limitations: Needs consensus expectations (not licensed here); sample decades old
notes: Phase F addition; relevant to the event monitor and to any announcement hypothesis

title: Intra-Day Seasonality in Activities of the Foreign Exchange Markets: Evidence From the Electronic Broking System
author: Ito, Hashimoto
source_type: journal (Journal of the Japanese and International Economies 20(4), 2006; NBER WP 12413)
summary: EBS firm quotes and transactions for USD/JPY and EUR/USD: U-shaped intraday activity and volatility for Tokyo and London participants but not New York; volatility and activity strongly positively correlated; volatility and bid-ask spread negatively correlated; deals and spread width negatively correlated in business hours.
extracted_hypotheses: Session effects in USD/JPY are about activity and spreads, not a profit signal by themselves
methodology: Intraday seasonality in EBS deals, price changes, spreads
limitations: Sample period not on the abstract page; interbank (EBS) not retail
notes: Phase F addition; core reference for Phase E session framework

title: What Prompts Japan to Intervene in the Forex Market? A New Approach to a Reaction Function
author: Ito, Yabu
source_type: journal (Journal of International Money and Finance 26(2), 2007; NBER WP 10456, May 2004)
summary: Daily Japanese intervention data 1 Apr 1991 - 31 Dec 2002; friction (cost-minimisation) model and ordered-probit reaction function: intervention shifted in June 1995 from frequent small operations to infrequent large ones; friction costs were lower in the first half.
extracted_hypotheses: Intervention likelihood rises with deviations from trend; the regime changed in June 1995
methodology: Ordered probit reaction function; noise-to-signal cut-off
limitations: Uses data disclosed after the fact; few events after 2004
notes: Phase F addition; supports a descriptive intervention event study, not a trading rule

title: Foreign Exchange Fixings and Returns Around the Clock
author: Krohn, Mueller, Whelan
source_type: working paper (Bank of Canada Staff WP 2021-48, Oct 2021); Journal of Finance 79(1) 2024 per a RePEc listing, journal page not opened
summary: Inter-dealer platform data: the US dollar tends to appreciate in the hours before the three major FX fixings and depreciate after them ('long and significant intraday drifts that reverse strongly at specific points during the day'), explained by pre-fixing order imbalances absorbed by dealers (inventory risk).
extracted_hypotheses: Time-of-day USD drift around fixings (e.g. the London 4pm fix) is a documented intraday pattern to test with reliable intraday data
methodology: Intraday returns around fixings; order-flow decomposition
limitations: Published 2024 (pattern documented in data before publication); requires reliable intraday timestamps; costs/spreads matter
notes: Phase F addition; directly relevant to session research once intraday data passes its tests

title: Trading Activity and Exchange Rates in High-Frequency EBS Data
author: Chaboud, Chernenko, Wright
source_type: working paper (Federal Reserve IFDP 903, September 2007; related JEEA 6(2-3) 2008)
summary: Five years of one-minute EBS data for EUR/USD and USD/JPY: a sharp pickup in trading volume follows US announcements even when data match expectations; at one-second frequency the price jumps immediately with little volume, then volume and volatility surge about 15 seconds later; UK holidays sharply reduce volume even among non-UK dealers.
extracted_hypotheses: Release-time price jumps happen within seconds (consistent with our per-second payroll test); volume is not driven only by news
notes: Phase F addition; supports the 0-5 s timing rule used in our data tests
